extracted.intended_audience: Commission Directorate-General staff responsible for designing and drafting evaluations, impact assessments, implementation strategies and related staff working documents
extracted.subtask_short: drafting EU evaluation and impact assessments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and quality standards for preparing Commission evaluation reports, impact assessment reports, and implementation strategies (staff working documents) to inform EU policymaking. Covers principles, required questions, report format, procedures (interservice work, RSB scrutiny), publication and minimum content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should cover at least the following criteria: effectiveness; efficiency; relevance; coherence; and EU added value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other criteria may be added as appropriate. The ‘evaluation findings’ part should be analytical and encompass these five evaluation criteria; evidence gathered on targeted questions addressing each criterion should feed into the narrative. Detailed analysis can be documented in Annex III (Evaluation matrix and answers to the evaluation questions (by evaluation criterion)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality (scope of evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the evaluation must be tailored to the particular intervention, the time since its implementation and the available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some criteria, new data will need to be collected, analysed and compared with other findings. For others, it is acceptable to produce a short summary on the basis of existing reports and information, or provide a standard explanation (e.g. where the EU has exclusive competence). In general, do not conduct an evaluation until at least 3 years’ reasonably full data are available where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Only independent and objective evaluations can deliver robust and reliable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis can be considered independent/objective (even if based on a contractor study) provided it is based on all relevant information, conducted without influence or pressure by third parties, and reports transparently on positive and negative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should be based on the best available evidence drawn from a diverse and appropriate range of methods and sources (triangulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all sources are equally robust; consider when/how evidence was collected and whether it is subject to bias or uncertainty. Where necessary, conduct sensitivity and/or scenario analysis to test robustness. Any limitations related to evidence and methodology, particularly regarding their ability to support conclusions, must be clearly explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations must make judgments on the basis of the available evidence and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments should be as specific as possible and the judgment criteria should be clearly identified in the design of the evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — What was the expected outcome of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the rationale for the intervention at the time it was prepared/adopted, the problem/needs and underlying causes, what it expected to achieve and how that achievement was to be assessed (the intervention logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on the impact assessment report (if available), explanatory memorandum and preamble of the final legal text. Include points of comparison against which the intervention will be assessed and, where possible, reference relevant UN SDGs the intervention aimed to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — How has the situation evolved over the evaluation period?
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a factual presentation of progress to date in implementing the intervention (both legally and on the ground).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section should present observed changes and implementation status without analysis-only assertions; feed factual evidence into analytical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — To what extent was the intervention successful and why? (effectiveness, efficiency, coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the expected situation with the actual situation; ‘success’ is assessed in terms of the extent to which an intervention achieves its objectives effectively, efficiently and coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments supporting the narrative should be clearly presented and referenced to any of the three criteria. Under effectiveness and efficiency, efforts should be made to address in quantitative terms benefits and costs. Analysis of efficiency should cover administrative and adjustment costs, simplification, and potential to reduce inefficiencies. Proportionality of costs and benefits should be assessed. Actual costs/benefits should be outlined in Annex IV (‘Overview of benefits and costs’) and where relevant a separate table on ‘Simplification and burden reduction’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — How did the EU intervention make a difference? (EU added value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an assessment of the intervention’s EU added value for individuals and businesses in the EU, going beyond restating legal reasons/objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present an ex post evidence-based assessment explaining clearly to whom the EU intervention made a difference and, where relevant, assess EU added value in different territories (rural, urban, cross-border, outermost regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — Is the intervention still relevant? (relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how well the objectives of the intervention reflected and still reflect current and future needs (continuing relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight mismatches between original objectives and current/future needs (consider strategic foresight) and explain reasons; this informs whether to maintain, adjust or terminate the intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions and lessons learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions should include an account of which elements of the intervention are (not) working and why; a summary of specific benefits that could not have been achieved without EU involvement; and credible evidence-based lessons and areas for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should investigate potential to simplify and reduce unnecessary costs; clearly reference lessons relating to REFIT issues such as regulatory/unnecessary burden, simplicity/complexity, efficiencies/inefficiencies and achievement of objectives at appropriate cost. Consider environmental and digital transition aspects where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interservice group involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: An interservice group should be set up and involved in all key steps of the evaluation work following validation, up to launch of interservice consultation and associated reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a public consultation is conducted (recommended for broad public interest evaluations and fitness checks), the interservice group should be involved in preparing the questionnaire. The interservice group should help identify relevant and significant impacts for impact assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Scrutiny Board (RSB) scrutiny and sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: For evaluations selected for scrutiny by the RSB, the draft report must be submitted to the RSB and the interservice consultation cannot be launched before the RSB has issued its opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the RSB opinion is negative, the lead DG(s) may submit a revised draft for a second opinion before proceeding. For impact assessments, a positive RSB opinion on the draft report is required before an initiative can proceed to interservice consultation; two negative opinions require VP responsible for better regulation to give green light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public access
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximise transparency and public access, the final evaluation report alongside the ‘call for evidence’, related consultation documents, and, if applicable, the contractor’s final study and the RSB opinion must be published centrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These documents must be published on the ‘Have Your Say’ web portal; the contractor’s study is published on the DG’s website. The RSB opinion(s) accompany the legislative proposal in decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feed into annual reporting and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: DGs must feed the evaluation results into their annual activity reports and identify follow-up actions in their annual management plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and sharing planned follow-up actions is part of accepting responsibility and accountability and ensures transparency. Follow-up can include impact assessments, improved guidance or further monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation report purpose and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead DG(s) prepares an evaluation report (a staff working document) presenting the analysis and answering the evaluation questions; the report communicates results and conclusions to policymakers and stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report should draw together all steps of the evaluation process, summarising and assessing the method applied, evidence collected and analysis conducted, on the basis of a wide range of sources. A template for format is available on GoPro.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation report quality: concise, non-technical, self-standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation report should be transparent, objective and balanced; concise (not longer than 50 pages of text accompanied by annexes); non-technical (accessible to non-expert readers); and self-standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must provide sufficient detail to enable the reader to follow the evidence and logic and to understand the conclusions without having to read supporting material (e.g. contractor study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder views and referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder views and how they have been considered should be the subject of transparent references throughout the report and summarised in the synopsis report (annex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All external material used (reports, scientific findings) should be systematically referenced. Explain/justify any significant differences between stakeholder views and the conclusions of the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary requirement (evaluations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no requirement to submit a report to the European Parliament and Council, prepare a short executive summary (max. 4-5 DGT pages) giving an accessible overview of headline findings and lessons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the executive summary available as a stand-alone staff working document in English, French and German.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annexes for detailed analysis and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed analysis should be provided in annexes: Annex III for Evaluation matrix and answers to evaluation questions (by evaluation criterion); Annex IV for ‘Overview of benefits and costs’ and simplification/burden reduction table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use annexes for more detailed and technical parts of the analysis to keep the main report focused and self-standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an impact assessment is required
rubrics_metrics.description: An impact assessment is required for Commission initiatives that are likely to have significant economic, environmental or social impacts or which entail significant spending, and where the Commission has a choice of policy options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All spending programmes, financial instruments and budgetary guarantees that entail significant expenditure (indicatively in excess of EUR 5 million) should be accompanied by an ex ante evaluation (financial statement). Where an impact assessment is required in principle but not possible, prepare an analytical staff working document within three months of adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact assessment work is led by the policy lead DG(s); DGs should establish early whether an impact assessment is required and seek political validation. An interservice group should steer the process and the RSB reviews the draft report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sufficient time to collect and analyse relevant evidence (data, scientific advice, expert views, stakeholder input). A positive RSB opinion on the draft impact assessment is required before interservice consultation. Following adoption, the impact assessment report is published on the Register of Commission Documents and ‘Have Your Say’ portal and transmitted to the legislator together with executive summary, subsidiarity grid, the adopted initiative and RSB opinion(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment key principles
rubrics_metrics.description: All impact assessments must be comprehensive, proportionate, evidence-based, open to stakeholders’ views, unbiased, prepared collectively with relevant Commission services, embedded in the policy cycle, transparent and of high quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles should guide the analysis and presentation; insights from strategic foresight and results of relevant evaluations and fitness checks should inform the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — What is the problem and why is it a problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the existence of a problem, identify who is affected, estimate the scale, analyse causes and consequences, and assess likelihood to persist absent EU policy (using foresight/scientific advice where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a revision, draw on the conclusions of the evaluation, if available. The answer should give policymakers the information needed to decide whether a policy response is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — Why should the EU act?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether Member States alone could resolve the issue satisfactorily, whether the EU has the right to act (legal basis) and whether it is best placed to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information policymakers need to decide whether an EU-level policy response is required; explain subsidiarity considerations (subsidiarity grid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — What should be achieved? (objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set out what the EU policy should achieve, clearly identify objectives including level of policy ambition, potential trade-offs, and criteria against which policy options and success will be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should take account of key long-term challenges and EU policy ambitions; these criteria will be used to compare options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — What are the options for achieving the objectives?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and screen available options to select the most relevant ones for analysis and comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of the process, present the most relevant policy options for further examination in the impact analysis stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — What are the economic, social and environmental impacts and who will be affected?
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out a robust assessment of economic, social and environmental impacts and of who will be affected and to what degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify relevant SDGs and, if feasible, how the initiative contributes to them. Assess impacts on SMEs, gender equality, fundamental rights, territories, non-EU countries, and essential security interests (including resilience against hybrid threats). Check conformity with ‘do no significant harm’ and ‘digital by default’ principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — How do the options compare (effectiveness, efficiency, coherence)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the options with regard to effectiveness, efficiency and coherence, compliance with proportionality and how future-proof they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess coherence with European Climate Law where appropriate; present relevant information to support decision-making and, where appropriate, suggest a preferred option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment question — How will monitoring and subsequent evaluation be organised?
rubrics_metrics.description: Set out arrangements for monitoring and ex post evaluation to track whether the policy measure delivers intended results and to inform future revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a set of indicators and relevant aspects of data collection to allow policymakers to know how the policy will be monitored and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on methods, evidence and analytical approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify appropriate methods for collecting/interpreting data and analysing impacts; use diverse sources and, where necessary, commission external studies or scientific advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess impacts qualitatively and quantitatively where possible; apply proportionate analysis but do not omit relevant information. Use a dynamic baseline, discount monetised estimates where appropriate, and analyse distributional effects and cumulative burdens. Include evidence to substantiate conclusions or explain why not (knowledge gaps/uncertainties) and signal limitations clearly and transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment report format and minimum content
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact assessment report should be transparent, objective and balanced; main report limited to 40 pages of text with annexes as appropriate and be written for non-expert readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final report must contain at least: description of social, economic and environmental impacts (and explicit statement if none considered significant); clear indication of who will be affected and how with quantification of costs and benefits; impacts on fundamental rights; impacts on SMEs and competitiveness; consideration of ‘do no significant harm’ and ‘digital by default’ principles; consistency with European Climate Law; assessment of impacts on relevant SDGs; and a detailed description of the consultation strategy and results (synopsis report). An executive summary (4-5 DGT pages) should be prepared as a separate linked staff working document and translated into all EU official languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory memorandum contents (link to impact assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For legislative and certain non-legislative proposals, the Commission’s political appreciation is set out in the explanatory memorandum accompanying the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanatory memorandum should cover: legal basis; subsidiarity; proportionality; results of evaluations and fitness checks; results of stakeholder consultations; short summary of input from external experts; summary of the impact assessment process including consultation of the RSB; regulatory fitness and simplification; conformity with EU Charter of Fundamental Rights; description of main impact categories; conformity with ‘do no significant harm’ and ‘digital by default’; assessment of contribution to relevant SDGs; and description of monitoring, evaluation and reporting arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation strategy — when required and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation strategies should be prepared for all major directives and regulations, but are normally not required for regulations or directives that already include provisions for tracking implementation, have a limited/technical scope, impose only one or a few legal obligations, or amend only one or a few existing obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sectoral DGs should assess potential difficulties affecting implementation and application by Member States, courts or enforcement agencies to decide where a strategy is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation strategy — required contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The implementation strategy should include all major steps the Commission should take when monitoring compliance of national laws with EU legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular it should identify the various types of support the Commission services will provide to assist Member States in transposition and implementation; and set out arrangements for monitoring implementation, including a timeline for the Commission’s compliance assessments, possible enforcement actions and implementation reports.
